title: Are all skills composed of knowledge?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou answers the objection that her skills-are-knowledge argument may hold for history but not for football, drama or even maths. Her reply is that every complex skill is composed of smaller units, which we call knowledge in academic subjects and sub-skills in practical ones, and that either way the skill must be taught by building up those units. She contrasts a generic-skills model, which practises the final performance repeatedly, with a deliberate-practice model built on a model of progression, using marathon training as her analogy. The real unresolved question, she says, is how to identify the right small steps. She proposes that this is an empirical assessment problem, using comparative judgement for the end goal and multiple-choice questions for the steps, while warning that correlation between a sub-skill and the final goal does not prove causation.
points: Knowledge and sub-skills are two labels for the same thing: the small units that a complex skill is built from and taught through.
Generic-skills models assume you acquire a skill by practising the whole performance, while deliberate-practice models break it down, as you do not train for a marathon by running marathons.
Endlessly re-fighting the skills-versus-knowledge debate blocks the more productive question of what the right small steps are, given how little research exists for most subjects.
Pairing comparative judgement of end-goal writing with multiple-choice checks on the steps could show which steps actually improve final performance.
A step that correlates with the end goal may not cause it, as the Yasso 800s example shows, so no single component should be taught exclusively.
quotes: Generic skills models assume you can acquire a skill directly, by practising the final skill over and over (eg writing an essay, playing an 11-a-side match). Deliberate practice models think you need to break the skill down into smaller steps (eg memorising chronologies, passing drills).
There are different labels for the small steps, but the crucial point is that both skills can be broken down into small steps and taught that way.
I also came back again and again to one of my favourite analogies, which is from a practical skill - marathon running. You don’t train for a marathon by running endless marathons.
It stops you from moving on to the far more important and productive next question, which is how do you know what the right “small steps” are?

Ultimately, it is an assessment question, and it is one that we at No More Marking are really interested in gathering empirical data on! We have two assessment techniques that can help. One is Comparative Judgement, which makes it easy to gather information on the end goal, particularly in subjects where the end goal involves writing. The second technique is multiple-choice questions, which can be used formatively to gather information on the steps on the way.

It’s tempting to say, let’s teach every student to answer this MCQ right and then they will all get better at writing. They might - but it might also turn out that performance on that MCQ and the extended writing are actually being caused by some other factor that we aren’t measuring.

My own take is that for complex skills like reading, writing, marathon running, etc., there is never going to be one component we can focus on exclusively. The whole point is that complex skills are made up of many sub-units. Data analysis can help us work out the best set of activities and the right amount of time to spend on each.
